title: The tests of Lehna
hook: tradition says a disciple named Lehna carried a bundle of wet grass and did every task the Guru asked without complaint

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kartarpur, the Creator's town, where the Guru took up a plow. He came home and farmed. Today, day forty-two, closes a week.

Somewhere near you there's a task nobody wants. The overflowing trash. The spreadsheet from 2014. The phone call to the angry customer. Sometimes one person just quietly does it. One day at Kartarpur, a man arrives in fine clothes. His name is Lehna, a trader from a nearby town, and tradition says that for years he led a band of pilgrims to a goddess temple in the hills. But on one journey, tradition says, he heard someone reciting Guru Nanak's hymn, the Japji, and couldn't get it out of his head. So he came to meet the man who wrote it. He found an old farmer in the fields.
screen: `THE TASK NOBODY WANTS.` → `A TRADER IN FINE CLOTHES.` → `HE HEARD THE JAPJI, AND CAME.`

segments.voice: Nanak was coming in from the fields with bundles of grass cut for the cattle, soaking wet and dripping mud. Lehna offered to carry one. It ruined his fine clothes. Tradition says the Guru's wife worried aloud about the stains, and Nanak answered that those weren't mud stains; they were saffron, the color of honor. The stories go on like that. The Guru asks for a muddy ditch to be cleared in the middle of the night; Lehna does it. A bowl falls into dirty water; Lehna climbs in after it. The Guru's own sons, tradition says, found reasons to refuse these tasks. Lehna didn't argue, didn't sulk, didn't point out how overqualified he was. He just did each thing, and did it well. Sikhs don't tell this as a story about a man who did whatever he was told. They tell it as a story about ego: the part of a person that says, this is beneath me. Lehna had been a leader with a following of his own. At Kartarpur he became a servant of servants, and that's exactly why he was trusted. Look back at the week: water thrown west at Hardwar, feet toward the Kaaba, a steady hand on the rock, the yogis on the mountain, Babur and a Guru who did not look away, Kartarpur and the plow, and now Lehna and the wet grass. The travels asked big questions. Kartarpur answered them with small, daily work, and in Lehna, the Guru found someone who understood.
screen: `WET GRASS ON FINE CLOTHES.` · `NOT MUD: SAFFRON.` · `THE DITCH, THE BOWL, THE NIGHT.` · `THE TEST WAS EGO.` · then, large: `JUST DO IT WELL.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the one task you've been putting off because it's boring, or dirty, or beneath you, and picture yourself doing it, carefully and well. If a little voice starts to grumble, don't argue with it; just let it talk while your hands work.
Lehna. The trader who carried wet grass, cleared a ditch at night, and climbed into dirty water, without complaint, before he became Guru Angad.
Your line: just do it well. Tomorrow, Kartarpur, 1539, and a sheet of flowers. Six weeks, done.

howItsDone: Sikhs tell the tests of Lehna as a teaching on seva, selfless service, and on setting aside ego; the story is often told to explain why Guru Nanak chose Lehna, not his sons, as his successor.

fork.setup: you arrive in fine clothes to meet a famous teacher. he's carrying a dripping bundle of wet grass. what do you do?
options: offer to carry it, clothes and all.
fork.reveal: Lehna carried it himself. when the mud stained his clothes, tradition says Nanak called the stains saffron, the color of honor.

original.note: Gurmukhi: Lehna, the name he had before he became the second Guru; tradition plays on lehna, what is owed, or due.

trapdoor: what you thought: a disciple who did chores.
what it means: a leader who became a servant, and a test not of obedience but of ego.
what a scholar hears: the tests come from later tradition, not the scripture, and are told to explain why Nanak passed over his sons for Lehna.

notes: Lehna led annual pilgrimages to the Jwalamukhi/Durga temple and heard Bhai Jodha reciting Japji: common tradition; confirm framing ('a goddess temple in the hills').
Wet grass and saffron: tradition attributes the worry to Mata Sulakhni; confirm.
Tests selected (the ditch at night, the bowl in dirty water) are among several in tradition; the corpse test is omitted deliberately. Confirm selection.
Pun on lehna (what is due) in the original note: confirm, or cut the note's second clause.
